description: Jesus as Messiah and Saviour; agape; incarnation, crucifixion, resurrection, ascension and atonement.
content_html:
Who Is Jesus Christ?

Christians use several titles to describe Jesus, each carrying deep theological meaning. Together they answer the question at the heart of Christianity: who was Jesus, and what did his life, death and resurrection achieve?

Messiah (from the Hebrew, meaning “anointed one”; in Greek, Christ) was the title Israel had long awaited — a king who would restore God’s rule. Christians believe Jesus fulfilled this role, though not through military conquest but through service and self-sacrifice. He is also called Son of God — expressing his divine identity — Lord, acknowledging his authority over all creation, and Saviour, pointing to his role in rescuing people from the consequences of sin.

Romans 3:23 states that “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” This establishes the universal need for a saviour: no human being is in right relationship with God by their own efforts.

Christian Love: Agape

Jesus’s teaching centres on love. The Greek word agape describes the kind of love Christians are called to practise: unconditional, self-giving and not dependent on the other person deserving it. The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) is the fullest single expression of Jesus’s ethical teaching — including the Beatitudes, love for enemies and commands about prayer, fasting and generosity.

In Matthew 22:36–39 Jesus summarises the whole law with the Two Great Commandments: love God with all your heart, soul and mind, and love your neighbour as yourself. The parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37) illustrates who “your neighbour” is: anyone in need, even an enemy. Agape has no boundaries.

The Incarnation

The incarnation is the belief that God became human in Jesus. Luke 1:26–35 records the angel Gabriel announcing to Mary that she would conceive a child by the Holy Spirit, who would be called “Son of the Most High.” This establishes Jesus’s unique origin: born of a human mother but conceived through the Spirit, he is both fully human and fully divine.

The incarnation matters enormously to Christians: God did not stay distant from human suffering but entered it. In Jesus, God experienced hunger, grief, temptation and death. This makes Jesus not only a divine saviour but also a compassionate intercessor who understands human weakness.

Key Fact

The four central events in Christian teaching about Jesus: the incarnation (God became human, Luke 1:26–35), the crucifixion (Jesus died on the cross, Mark 15:21–41), the resurrection (Jesus rose from the dead, Matthew 28:1–10), and the ascension (Jesus returned to heaven, Acts 1:9–11).

The Crucifixion, Resurrection and Ascension

The crucifixion is described in Mark 15:21–41. Jesus was nailed to a cross and died. For Christians, this was not a defeat but the central saving act of history: Jesus “paying the price” for human sin. The curtain of the Temple tore at the moment of his death — a sign that the barrier between God and humanity had been removed.

The resurrection is the claim that Jesus rose from the dead. Matthew 28:1–10 records Mary Magdalene and other women discovering the empty tomb and encountering the risen Jesus. Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15 that without the resurrection, Christian faith is “useless.” For most Christians, the resurrection is a bodily event — not merely a spiritual experience — that proves Jesus is the Son of God and that death does not have the final word.

The ascension (Acts 1:9–11) marks Jesus returning to the Father. He promises to send the Holy Spirit, and the disciples are told he will return in the same way he left — pointing to the Second Coming.

Salvation and Atonement

Salvation is the central purpose of Jesus’s death and resurrection. The word means being rescued or delivered. Christians believe human beings cannot save themselves — Romans 3:23 and Romans 6:23 (“the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus”) together establish the problem and the solution.

Atonement (literally “at-one-ment”) describes how Jesus’s death bridges the gap between sinful humanity and a holy God. A key image is substitution: Jesus pays the debt or penalty that human sin incurs. Romans 3:24 speaks of being “justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus.”

Ephesians 2:8–9 is another key passage: “it is by grace you have been saved, through faith — and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God.” This verse teaches that salvation is entirely God’s initiative (grace), not something humans achieve by good works.

Key Fact

Three key salvation verses: Romans 3:23 (“all have sinned”), Romans 6:23 (“the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life”), Ephesians 2:8–9 (“by grace you have been saved, through faith — not from yourselves, it is the gift of God”). These establish sin as universal, death as its consequence, and grace as the only solution.

All mainstream Christian denominations agree that salvation comes through Jesus Christ, but they differ on how it works in practice. Roman Catholics teach that salvation is received through faith and the sacraments (especially baptism and the Eucharist), and that ongoing participation in the life of the Church is necessary. Many Protestant traditions, following the Reformation, emphasise “faith alone” (sola fide): salvation is received by trusting in Jesus, not by performing religious acts. Evangelical Christians stress the need for a personal decision to accept Jesus as Lord and Saviour — a moment of conversion.

The resurrection is not merely a historical claim for most Christians — it shapes how they live. Easter Sunday is the holiest day in the Christian calendar. The resurrection promises that death is not the end, giving Christians hope in the face of bereavement and suffering. Paul writes that Christians will one day share in a resurrection like Christ’s. The resurrection also validates Jesus’s teaching: if he rose, then his claims about himself and about God are trustworthy.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain’ questions on salvation and atonement, always reference at least one named scripture. Romans 3:23, Romans 6:23 and Ephesians 2:8–9 are the three key texts listed for this topic — knowing all three will allow you to cover ‘all have sinned’, ‘the wages of sin is death’ and ‘saved by grace’. A common error is confusing the incarnation (God becoming human) with the resurrection (Jesus rising from death) — keep these distinct. For the 15-mark ‘Discuss’ on topics like the resurrection or salvation, present both the importance of the belief and challenges to or alternative understandings of it. Remember that SPaG marks are awarded in extended responses, so practise spelling ‘incarnation’, ‘atonement’, ‘resurrection’ and ‘ascension’ accurately.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christians describe Jesus using the titles Messiah (anointed one), Son of God, Lord and Saviour; his teaching on agape love is expressed in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) and the Two Great Commandments (Matthew 22:36–39).
  • The four central events are the incarnation (Luke 1:26–35), crucifixion (Mark 15:21–41), resurrection (Matthew 28:1–10) and ascension (Acts 1:9–11), each shaping Christian worship and belief.
  • Salvation (rescue from sin) and atonement (restored relationship with God) are achieved through Jesus; key texts are Romans 3:23–24, Romans 6:23 and Ephesians 2:8–9, all stressing that salvation is a free gift of grace, not earned by human effort.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the resurrection is important for Christians.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- The resurrection proves Jesus is the Son of God and validates his teaching; Paul writes that without the resurrection faith is 'useless' (1 Corinthians 15). [up to 3 marks]
- The resurrection gives Christians hope that death is not the end; Matthew 28:1-10 shows Jesus risen, and Christians believe they will share in resurrection. [up to 3 marks]
- The resurrection demonstrates God's power over sin and death, confirming that atonement has been accomplished.
- Romans 6:23 links eternal life directly to Jesus, whose resurrection makes that life possible. [3 marks per point: 1 simple, 2 developed, 3 developed with source]

practice_questions.text: 'The crucifixion is more important than the resurrection for Christian belief.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- The crucifixion is the atoning act: Jesus pays the penalty for sin (Romans 3:24), making forgiveness possible.
- Romans 6:23 says 'the wages of sin is death' — the crucifixion is where that wage is paid on humanity's behalf.
- Mark 15:21-41 describes the tearing of the Temple curtain at Jesus's death, symbolising access to God restored.
- Some theologians argue the act of atonement is completed on the cross: 'It is finished' (John 19:30).

Arguments against / alternative views:
- Paul writes that without the resurrection 'your faith is futile' (1 Corinthians 15) — the resurrection confirms the crucifixion was not a defeat.
- The resurrection is the basis for Christian hope of life after death (Matthew 28:1-10).
- The ascension (Acts 1:9-11) follows the resurrection: without it, Jesus is not at the Father's right hand interceding for believers.
- Many Christians would say both are equally important: the death and resurrection together form one saving event that cannot be separated.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified personal conclusion about which is more important or whether they are inseparable.
Secure: Both sides present with at least one source; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources; conclusion present but not fully weighed.
Emerging: One-sided or brief; no real use of sources.

practice_questions.marks: The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5-7) calls Christians to love even their enemies and to treat others as they wish to be treated [1]; it sets out the values of God's kingdom including mercy, peacemaking and generosity [1]. [1 mark per valid point, max 2]

glossary_terms.definition: The Hebrew word for 'anointed one'; in Greek, Christos. Christians believe Jesus is the long-awaited Messiah promised by the prophets.
A title for Jesus expressing his unique relationship with God the Father and his divine nature.
A title for Jesus affirming his authority and divine sovereignty.
A title for Jesus meaning he rescues humanity from sin and its consequences.
Unconditional, self-giving love; the kind of love God shows to humanity and which Jesus commands Christians to show to others.
The extended teaching of Jesus in Matthew chapters 5 to 7, setting out the values and ethics of God's kingdom.
The belief that God the Son took on human flesh in the person of Jesus; God became fully human while remaining fully divine.
The death of Jesus on a Roman cross; Christians believe it was an atoning sacrifice for the sins of humanity.
The belief that Jesus rose bodily from the dead on the third day after his crucifixion, vindicating his claims and defeating death.
The belief that after his resurrection Jesus was taken up into heaven to reign at the right hand of God the Father.
Being rescued from the consequences of sin and restored to a right relationship with God; achieved through Jesus Christ.
The means by which Jesus's death bridges the gap between sinful humanity and a holy God; making 'at-one-ment' between God and people.
Undeserved favour; God's free gift of forgiveness and salvation, not earned by human effort.
